newsitem.title: INDIA: Scions of India's Thapar group fight for own turf.
newsitem.headline: Scions of India's Thapar group fight for own turf.

text.p: It has taken only six years of a liberalised economy for the cracks to start showing in the 60-year-old Thapar family empire.
For almost six decades, the family had flourished with interests ranging from paper and chemicals to colour picture tubes and electric fans.
It thrived under a socialist regime that used licences to control competition.
Today, after six years of heated competition from Indian and foreign firms and with many of the group's businesses going downhill, the scions are fighting to carve up the empire.
Patriarch L.M. Thapar, chairman of the flagship Ballarpur Industries Ltd (BILT), a paper and chemical maker, said there was no decision yet to divide up the spoils.

"Each business needs to be independent of the other. Each company has to be more efficient in the new perspective. We are looking at our core competencies, but the exercise might take a few months," he told Reuters in an interview.

Last year McKinsey and Co advised the Thapar group to concentrate on its core businesses of paper and chemicals, and wind up its interests in food processing, footwear manufacturing and loss-making edible oils.
Thapar said: "I will make a comment only when we seek shareholders approval."
Along with BILT, the Thapar group includes Bharat Starch Ltd, Greaves Ltd, Crompton Greaves Ltd and Andhra Pradesh Rayon Ltd.

The Business Standard newspaper recently said L.M. Thapar's family situation increased the likelihood of a split-up of BILT and its associated companies. The patriarch has no children, and three of his nephews want separate business empires, it said.
The daily said following a split, the empire could resemble that of textile maker JCT Ltd, run by L.M. Thapar's brother, M.M. Thapar. The sons of M.M. Thapar have clearly demarcated roles in JCT.
The Business Standard said one of L.M. Thapar's nephews would get BILT's paper business.

Another would take Andhra Pradesh Rayon and the non-paper business of BILT such as edible oils, The Pioneer newspaper and food processing. The third would receive Greaves Ltd, Crompton Greaves Ltd and Bharat Starch Ltd.
Analysts feel the split has been long in coming and the only chance for survival.
Corporate consultant Mrityunjay Athreya said: "Indian groups have to concentrate on one or two areas. They cannot be all things to all businesses and hope to be successful in all."
He said a group like the Thapars should have no more than two core businesses to compete globally.

"The Thapars have been confused at the top, and this split is just hastening a confrontation at the top level between the nephews of L.M. Thapar," said an analyst at Citibank, who asked not to be identified.
He said Andhra Pradesh Rayon and BILT's paper businesses should have been merged long ago for synergy, but even in the proposed split they were being kept apart.
The Thapar group has consistently disappointed investors, the analyst said.
"When the going was good, BILT and other Thapar companies would raise money and then invest it in each other for cross-holdings. They never, ever concentrated on creating wealth for shareholders."

BILT's net profit plummeted to 380 million rupees in 1996/97 (April-March) from 1.02 billion rupees in 1995/96. JCT Ltd reported a net loss of 69.6 million rupees in 1995/96 compared to a net profit of 599.7 million rupees in 1994/95.

Crompton Greaves Ltd's net profit fell to 307.6 million rupees in 1996/97 from 640.4 million rupees the previous year. JCT Electronics Ltd's net profit was expected to fall to about 50 million rupees in 1996/97 from 152 million rupees in the previous year, a company official said in May.

The analyst said only Greaves Ltd and Crompton Greaves had a good chance of being profitable in the years to come. "In many of the other companies, it is likely that shareholders will throw the Thapars out of the management."

A senior Thapar group executive said: "The group has consistently found funds harder to come by. Banks and financial institutions are willing to lend only to Indian blue chips or government firms. Where do you go when you are neither?"
